evidence_set: Stockholm, 1985–1996: the inventory included deaths involving illicit drugs or non-prescribed morphine/methadone and deaths of people with a personal history of drug use problems, regardless of whether acute poisoning caused death. It contained 1,061 forensic and 151 hospital cases (1,212 total). NMR/Stockholm included 761 of the 1,212 inventory deaths and 734 of the 1,061 forensic cases. For the 151 hospital deaths, mainly in people with HIV who used drugs, the paper prints 28% captured; subtracting 734 from 761 gives 27, and 27/151 is 17.9%, so the printed percentage is not reconcilable from those counts. NMR/Stockholm also included 419 deaths absent from the inventory; 30 were confirmed inventory omissions, comprising 21 Stockholm residents who died elsewhere and nine administrative omissions. The paper describes 49 other deaths involving drowning, pharmaceutical drugs or alcohol, and seven with no cause found, without describing every remaining certificate-only death. The inventory is therefore neither complete nor an independent standard for true drug-caused deaths. Table I prints 1,181 NMR/Stockholm deaths, one more than 761+419=1,180. The paper also says Toxreg included 317 of 454 inventory deaths in 1994–1996, then says 43 of the 317 Toxreg cases were absent from the inventory because findings suggested medical treatment; these contradictory descriptions do not establish an unambiguous 317-overlap-plus-43 count. Independent arithmetic gives 1,212−761=451 inventory cases absent from NMR and 419−30=389 other NMR cases, but neither quantity is a validated number of missed or falsely attributed drug-poisoning deaths. Using inventory membership alone, 761/1,212=62.8% capture and 761/(761+419)=64.5% positive predictive value; the paper prints 64.5% as sensitivity and 62.8% as positive predictive value. These appear interchanged under those denominators, but the inconsistent totals and subsequent inventory omissions prevent treating the printed accuracy measures as validated causal accuracy estimates.

Datasets and inventory definitions, Table I and Methods (pp. 3–4); Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory (p. 5); Discussion limitations and dataset differences (pp. 7–8)

The National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (NPSUM) receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales, including causes of death and full toxicology reports. The consulting toxicologist evaluates detected substances for likely involvement; this is more than drug detection alone. For each opioid and year, the authors classified NPSUM cases according to whether that opioid was specifically named in a cause-of-death field or an ambiguous drug-related cause was given with the opioid implicated as causative by the consulting toxicologist. They divided ONS counts by the NPSUM named share to project national totals, without linking individual deaths. In 2011, 122 of 416 NPSUM heroin/morphine deaths had ambiguous causes (29.3%); the paper reports that 574 ONS deaths yielded a projected 813. Independent arithmetic using the exact printed counts gives 574/(294/416)=812.2 rather than 813, so 813 is retained as the paper’s reported estimate. In 2022, the paper reports 1,264 ONS deaths versus a projected 1,980 (36% of the projection uncounted). For 2011–2022, ONS count versus reported projection (rounded share of projection uncounted) was heroin/morphine 13,471 versus 20,323 (34%); methadone 5,752 versus 9,444 (39%); tramadol 2,455 versus 3,865 (36%); dihydrocodeine 1,201 versus 1,854 (35%); codeine 1,886 versus 2,859 (34%); fentanyl 599 versus 887 (32%). Multiple drugs were detected in 16,101 of 16,628 NPSUM opioid-related deaths (96.8%). The paper states that ONS identifies specific opioids from cause-of-death fields in the Record of Inquest; it does not explicitly describe searching or excluding a separate conclusion entry. Heroin and morphine are combined. Table 1 gives projected heroin/morphine 95% intervals of 813 (767–868) in 2011, 1,980 (1,894–2,074) in 2022 and 20,323 (19,382–21,358) over all years. The abstract instead gives 765–866 for 2011, and Results gives 1,895–2,075 for 2022; Table 1 values are used here. Applying the stated Wilson method to the printed 2011 NPSUM counts independently yields transformed endpoints 766.94–868.05, rounding to 767–868. Other annual NPSUM denominators and supplements were not supplied, so the 2022 and aggregate intervals were not independently regenerated. These intervals address sampling uncertainty in programme proportions, not representativeness, the unlinked projection or causal-attribution assumptions. Reports from over 90% of coroners do not imply complete case coverage, and the 29% and 36% endpoint shares do not give the full annual range.

Among accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to NP-SAD in 2000, two researchers independently identified and classified 1,037 cases, with a medical consultant confirming case identification and categories. Suicide verdicts, open verdicts with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, cases with no verdict and cases with insufficient information for a causal judgment were excluded. They classified 802 (77%) as direct acute overdose; other categories were traumatic accidents (31), toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition (40), toxicity with a drug-related medical condition (72), acute infections (18), and acute non-traumatic physical events (74). In the last group, aspiration was mentioned in 42 direct-aspiration-asphyxia cases and 22 aspiration-pneumonia cases; not all 74 were aspiration deaths. Medical-condition and infection categories were separate from acute physical events. Independent arithmetic gives 802/1,037=77.3%, 40+72=112 medical-condition cases, and all six category counts sum to 1,037. Methods classified recent drug use with no evidence of another cause as accidental direct overdose by default. The authors do not call the 77% share an upper limit; that would be an editorial interpretation of their classification rule, not a reported finding or validated bound. The final Discussion says that when a substance was not reported it was unclear whether it was absent at post-mortem testing or had not been tested for, and that including negative findings would help. No linked comparison with official statistics or ICD-coded overdose totals was made. This describes classification within a broader drug-related register, not a measured false-positive rate for official overdose statistics.

evidence_set: For combined heroin/morphine deaths in England and Wales, ONS identified 574 deaths in 2011. NPSUM held 416 heroin/morphine-related deaths, of which 122 (29.3%) had ambiguous drug-related causes with the opioid implicated as causative by the consulting toxicologist. The paper reports a projected national total of 813 (Table 1/Results 95% interval 767–868), describing about 29% of projected deaths as uncounted. Using the exact printed NPSUM counts independently gives 574/(294/416)=812.2 rather than 813; 813 is the paper’s reported point estimate. Its stated Wilson method gives transformed 2011 endpoints 766.94–868.05 from 122/416, which round to the Table 1 interval. In 2022, ONS counted 1,264 against a reported projection of 1,980, or 36% of the projection uncounted. Over 2011–2022, ONS counted 13,471 against a reported projection of 20,323: independent arithmetic gives 33.7% of the projection uncounted and a projection 50.9% above ONS. The median number of drugs detected at post-mortem in NPSUM heroin/morphine deaths rose from four in 2011 to six in 2022 (Fig. 1A); detection does not establish that each drug caused death. Individual deaths were not linked. Both sources combine heroin and morphine, so this comparison does not measure morphine named instead of heroin. The paper states that ONS uses cause-of-death fields on the Record of Inquest but does not explicitly describe searching or excluding a separate conclusion entry. NPSUM uses the consulting toxicologist’s evaluation in the toxicology report; the paper does not establish that person’s employment status. Table 1 gives projected-count intervals of 1,894–2,074 for 2022 and 19,382–21,358 for all years. The 2011 abstract instead gives 765–866, and the 2022 Results gives 1,895–2,075; Table 1 values are retained here. The other annual programme denominators and supplements were not supplied, so the 2022 and aggregate intervals were transcribed rather than independently regenerated. These intervals address sampling uncertainty in programme shares, not representativeness or causal accuracy. The 29% and 36% figures are endpoint years, not annual extremes.

The NAME expert panel states that 6-acetylmorphine in a biological sample is sufficient evidence to ascribe intoxication to heroin; that sentence has no attached citation. Later in the same paragraph, the panel treats a blood morphine-to-codeine ratio greater than one as possible evidence of heroin use, with references 44–45 attached to that statement, and adds the context of scene paraphernalia with reference 46. The reference list identifies studies on ratios in people investigated for impaired driving, ratios in heroin-related poisoning deaths, and identifying heroin toxicity when 6-acetylmorphine is not detected. The position paper does not report diagnostic accuracy for this rule. Those empirical studies were not independently read here; confirming their citations is not independent validation of the rule.
